items.prompt: How many lines does a standard musical staff have?
rubric: A standard staff has five lines and four spaces.
Four is the number of spaces (or lines in some older chant notation).

items.prompt: Which note letter names are used in Western music before the pattern repeats?
rubric: Seven letters A-G repeat.
A to H is used in some German naming for B natural, not the standard English system.

items.prompt: In 4/4 time, what does the top number tell you?

options.label: Number of measures in the piece

rubric: The top number gives beats per measure.
The bottom number gives the note value that gets the beat.

items.prompt: What is the term for the distance between two notes?
rubric: An interval is the distance between two pitches.
An octave is one specific interval.

items.prompt: How many notes make up a basic triad?
rubric: A triad has three notes: root, third, fifth.
Four notes would be a seventh chord.

items.prompt: Which of these are note values found in standard notation? Select all that apply.
rubric: Quarter, half and eighth notes are standard values.
There is no tenth note; values divide by powers of two.

items.prompt: A friend hands you a score and asks what the symbol at the far left of each staff, which looks like a fancy ampersand-like curl, is called. It fixes which pitches the lines and spaces represent. What is it?
rubric: The curling symbol is the treble (G) clef.
The bass clef looks like a backward C with two dots.

items.prompt: Why does a sharp sign placed before a note change how it sounds?

options.label: It raises the pitch by a semitone
It makes the note last longer
It lowers the pitch by a semitone

rubric: A sharp raises pitch by a semitone.
A flat lowers it; dynamics and duration are separate.

items.prompt: What best explains the difference between a major and a minor triad?

options.label: The fifth is a semitone lower in minor
Minor adds a fourth note to the chord
The third is a semitone lower in minor
The root is a tone lower in minor

rubric: Minor has a lowered (minor) third.
Lowering the fifth gives a diminished triad.

items.prompt: A piece has a key signature of no sharps or flats. Which key is it most likely in?
rubric: No accidentals means C major (or A minor).
G has one sharp and F has one flat.

items.prompt: A dotted half note in 4/4 time lasts how many beats?
rubric: A dot adds half the value: 2 + 1 = 3.
2.5 comes from wrongly adding a quarter of the value.

items.prompt: What does a rest in a score tell the performer?

options.label: Stay silent for a set duration

rubric: A rest marks silence of a specific length.
A tie or fermata extends notes; a rest does not.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe a major scale? Select all that apply.

options.label: Its eighth note is the same letter as the first
Its step pattern is whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
It has seven different notes before the octave repeats
It always begins on the note C

rubric: The major scale has seven notes, a fixed pattern, and repeats at the octave.
It can start on any note, not just C.

items.prompt: A beginner sees two songs, one marked 3/4 and one marked 4/4. They tap along and ask how the feel differs. One is a waltz-like song and one a steady march. What best explains the difference?

options.label: 3/4 uses three notes in each chord
3/4 groups beats in threes; 4/4 in fours

rubric: Time signature sets beats per measure, giving different groupings.
It does not set speed, chord size or total length.

items.prompt: A piece is in C major. Which minor key shares exactly the same key signature (no sharps or flats)?
rubric: A minor is the relative minor, built on the sixth degree of C major, so it shares the signature.
E minor and D minor are also diatonic to C major but are not its relative minor; C minor has three flats.

items.prompt: A song is in 6/8 and is felt in the usual way. How is the bar best understood?

options.label: Four beats, each divided into three eighths
Two beats, each divided into three eighths
Six equal beats, each divided into two
Three beats, each divided into two eighths

rubric: 6/8 is compound duple: two dotted-quarter beats, each split into three eighths.
Counting six beats or three beats treats it like simple time and ignores the grouping in threes.

items.prompt: In 4/4, where the quarter note gets one beat, how long does a dotted quarter note last?
rubric: A dot adds half the note's value, so a quarter plus an eighth equals one and a half beats.
Two beats confuses the dot with doubling the value.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a C minor triad and a C major triad?

options.label: The fifth is lowered by a semitone
The third is raised by a whole tone
The third is lowered by a semitone
The root is lowered by a semitone

rubric: The minor triad has a minor third, one semitone lower than the major third.
Lowering the fifth gives a diminished triad, not a minor one.

items.prompt: What does a tie between two notes on the staff tell the performer?

options.label: Play two different notes smoothly without a break
Play the two notes as one sustained sound of combined length
Shorten the second note to half of its written value
Repeat the previous bar once before moving on

rubric: A tie joins notes of the same pitch into one note with the combined duration.
A slur joins different pitches smoothly; ties are often confused with slurs.

items.prompt: In the key of C major, which of these diatonic triads are minor chords? Select all that apply.
rubric: The ii, iii and vi chords of a major key are minor: Dm, Em and Am.
F and G are the major IV and V chords.

items.prompt: A student looks at a folk tune with one flat in the key signature. The melody mostly circles around D, the chords are Dm, Gm and A, and the tune ends on a D minor chord. Which key best describes the tune?

options.label: Bb major, because it has a flat in the signature
D minor, because the music centres on D and ends there
F major, because the signature has one flat
G minor, because Gm is the central chord

rubric: One flat fits F major or D minor; the melody and final chord on D show the tonal centre is D minor.
Choosing F major reads only the signature and ignores where the music resolves.

items.prompt: Using the major scale pattern (whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half), which note is the seventh degree of A major?
rubric: A major has three sharps: F#, C# and G#, so the seventh degree is G#.
G natural is the seventh of the A mixolydian or natural minor, not major.

items.prompt: A melody outlines the notes C E G. Transposing it up a perfect fifth gives which notes?
rubric: A perfect fifth above C is G, E rises to B and G rises to D, keeping a major triad.
G Bb D changes the quality to minor.

items.prompt: A bar of 4/4 already contains a dotted half note. Which single note value completes the bar?
rubric: A dotted half lasts three beats, so one beat remains, which is a quarter note.
A half note would give five beats, a common miscount of the dot.

items.prompt: What is the interval from C up to A?
rubric: C to A spans six letter names and nine semitones, a major sixth.
Minor sixth would be C to Ab; C to G is the fifth.

items.prompt: In the key of F major, which chord is the dominant (V) chord?
rubric: The fifth degree of F major is C, and its diatonic triad is C major (C E G).
Bb major is IV; G would be V only in the key of C.

items.prompt: In the key of G major, which of these chords are major triads that belong to the key? Select all that apply.
rubric: G, C and D are the I, IV and V chords of G major.
A and E major need C# and G#, which are not in G major; A minor and E minor are the diatonic forms.

items.prompt: A singer finds a song too high. It is in C major with chords C, F and G. She wants it lowered by a whole step, to Bb major, keeping the same chord functions. Which chords should the guitarist play?
rubric: Lowering each chord by a whole step turns C, F, G into Bb, Eb and F, keeping I, IV, V.
Moving only the first chord, or raising by a step, leaves the functions wrong.

items.prompt: A melody uses the notes C D E G. You transpose it up a major third. Which set of notes results?
rubric: A major third above C is E, and every note moves up four semitones, giving E F# G# B.
Distractors shift by a minor third or by the wrong number of semitones, or keep the original scale-step pattern.

items.prompt: In the key of A major, which notes spell the dominant seventh chord (V7)?
rubric: V in A major is E; the dominant seventh is E G# B D, using the key's G# and a minor seventh D.
Distractors use a minor triad, a raised seventh, or build the chord on the tonic.

items.prompt: A piece in 6/8 is played at a moderate tempo in its usual feel. How many main beats are felt per bar, and which note value carries each beat?
rubric: 6/8 is compound duple: two beats per bar, each a dotted quarter (three eighths).
Distractors count the subdivisions as beats or treat it as simple time.

items.prompt: Which notes spell a D minor seventh chord (Dm7)?
rubric: Minor seventh chord = minor triad D F A plus a minor seventh, C.
Distractors use a major third or a major seventh, giving D, Dmaj7, or minor-major seventh sounds.

items.prompt: What is the interval from F# up to the D above it?
rubric: F# to D# would be a major sixth, so F# to D is a minor sixth (eight semitones).
Distractors come from ignoring the sharp or miscounting semitones.

items.prompt: Which of these chords are diatonic triads in G major? Select all that apply.
rubric: G major has the triads G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F#dim, so Bm, Em and C belong.
F major and D minor need F natural, which is not in G major.

items.prompt: A guitarist places a capo on fret 3 and plays the open chord shapes G, C and D for a song. A singer asks which key the song now sounds in. The capo raises every pitch by three semitones.
rubric: G raised three semitones is Bb, so the shapes G, C, D sound as Bb, Eb, F in Bb major.
Distractors ignore the capo, miscount semitones, or take the subdominant as the key.

items.prompt: A song in A minor uses the progression Am, Dm, E, Am. Why is the V chord a major E rather than E minor?

options.label: The E chord needs the G natural of the key signature
E major is borrowed from the relative key of C major
Major chords are always used for the dominant in minor keys
The G# serves as a leading tone that pulls up to A

rubric: The raised seventh (G#) from harmonic minor creates a leading tone resolving to the tonic.
Distractors misattribute E major to the relative major or claim a general rule that ignores the leading tone.

items.prompt: In the key of C major, a progression goes C, Am, D7, G. What is the function of the D7 chord?

options.label: Dominant seventh of the home key
Secondary dominant that leads to V

rubric: D7 contains F#, which is outside C major, and resolves to G, so it is V7/V.
Distractors confuse it with the home dominant, a borrowed chord, or a subdominant.

items.prompt: A student labels the chord D F# A C as Dmaj7. What is wrong with this analysis?

options.label: The chord is a D minor seventh with a raised third
The F# should be F natural for a seventh chord
The A should be raised to A# in a seventh chord
The C natural is a minor seventh, so it is D7

rubric: A major triad plus a minor seventh (C natural) is a dominant seventh, D7; Dmaj7 would need C#.
Distractors misread the third or the fifth of the chord.

items.prompt: A G7 chord contains the tritone B–F. When G7 resolves to C major, how do these two notes move most smoothly?

options.label: B down to Bb, F down to E
B up to C, F down to E
B up to C, F up to G
B down to A, F up to G

rubric: The tritone resolves inward-to-outward by step: the leading tone B rises to C and the seventh F falls to E.
Distractors resolve in the wrong directions or alter the tones.

items.prompt: A song modulates from C major to G major. Which chord works as a pivot, since it is diatonic in both keys?
rubric: Am is vi in C major and ii in G major, so it belongs to both keys.
F and Dm contain F natural, not found in G major, and D major is not diatonic in C major.

items.prompt: A passage has no sharps or flats in its key signature. Which observations suggest it is in A minor rather than C major? Select all that apply.

options.label: Phrases settle on an Am chord as the point of rest
C major appears often as a chord
G# accidentals rise by step to A before cadences
The key signature has no sharps or flats

rubric: Resting on A and using G# as a leading tone point to A as tonic.
The key signature and frequent C major chords are shared by both relative keys and do not distinguish them.

items.prompt: A song is in C major. Its bridge uses Fm and then Bb7 before returning to C. A bandmate says the chords sound dark but still connected to the home key. Which analysis best explains them?

options.label: They are borrowed from the parallel minor, C minor
They come from the Lydian mode on C
They modulate temporarily to F major
They are secondary dominants of the relative minor

rubric: Fm is iv and Bb is bVII in C minor, so this is modal mixture from the parallel minor.
Distractors misname the source: F major lacks the Ab of Fm, and Lydian would use F# not Ab/Bb.

items.prompt: In C major, an arranger swaps the tonic chord C for Am in the middle of a progression and the harmony still feels stable. What best explains why the substitution works?

options.label: Am is the dominant of C, so it resolves to the tonic as well
Both contain the leading tone B, so they pull in the same way
They share the root note A, so the bass line still points home
They share two notes, C and E, so Am keeps a tonic-like sound

rubric: C and E are common to both chords, so Am keeps tonic function as a relative-minor substitute.
Distractors confuse shared roots or invent a dominant or leading-tone link; Am contains neither B nor a dominant relationship to C.

items.prompt: A tune in A minor moves from Dm to E major (E–G#–B) and then back to Am, with G# sounding in the melody just before the final A. Which analysis of the G# is best?

options.label: A chromatic passing tone with no harmonic role, because G# is foreign to every A minor chord
The natural seventh of A minor, so E is just a minor v chord written with a wrong accidental
A sign of modulation to E major, because G# belongs to E major, so the key has changed for good
A raised seventh from harmonic minor, which gives a leading tone and makes E a true dominant

rubric: G# is the raised 7th of harmonic minor; it creates a leading tone and a major V chord leading to i.
Distractors treat G# as incidental, confuse it with the natural 7th (G natural), or read one borrowed note as a full modulation.

items.prompt: In C major, a phrase ends C/G (C major chord with G in the bass) – G7 – C. How should the C/G chord be analysed?

options.label: As a IV chord in disguise, because a G bass makes the harmony subdominant in function
As a first-inversion tonic, so the bass simply steps toward the dominant on its way home
As a tonic in second inversion, so the phrase has already closed before the G7 arrives
As a cadential six-four: it decorates the dominant, and its C and E fall to B and D

rubric: The cadential six-four sounds over the dominant bass and resolves C to B and E to D, so it functions as V, not I.
Distractors read it by its chord name or inversion alone and ignore its dominant function.

items.prompt: A melody centres on D, uses the notes D E F G A B C with no accidentals, and rests on a D minor chord. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: D Dorian, since the natural B above a D minor triad gives the raised sixth
D Mixolydian, since the tune ends on D and uses no sharps in its scale
D Phrygian, since the note E sits just above the tonic and colours the line
D natural minor, since the F natural makes the third minor and nothing else matters

rubric: Minor third with natural sixth (B) over D is Dorian; the notes are the C major collection centred on D.
Distractors ignore the sixth degree: natural minor needs Bb, Mixolydian needs a major third (F#), and Phrygian needs Eb.

items.prompt: In C major, a jazz pianist plays Db7 in place of G7 before resolving to C. What explains why this tritone substitution works?

options.label: Both chords contain the pitch class G, so Db7 inherits the dominant's function directly
Db is a fifth below G, so Db7 resolves into C by the same root motion as G7
Both chords contain the same tritone (B/Cb and F), and the Db root slides down a semitone to C
Both chords are built on the fifth degree, so Db7 resolves like a normal V7 would

rubric: G7 and Db7 share the tritone B–F (enharmonically Cb–F), and the tritone's resolution plus the descending semitone bass supply the dominant pull.
Distractors invoke root relationships or a shared note that the substitute chord does not actually have.

items.prompt: In C major, which of these chords contain the tritone formed by B and F? Select all that apply.
rubric: G7 (G B D F) and B diminished (B D F) both contain B and F, a diminished fifth apart.
Dm7, Fmaj7 and Cmaj7 each contain only one of the two notes, so they have no B–F tritone.

items.prompt: The verse of a song in C major goes C – E7 – Am – F, then returns to C at the chorus with no other accidentals. A bandmate asks what the E7 (E–G#–B–D) is doing there. Which analysis best accounts for it?

options.label: A chord borrowed from C minor, since E7 shares its third with the parallel minor key
A notation mistake, because E major is not diatonic and the chord should be Em7
A secondary dominant, V7 of vi: G# is a temporary leading tone to A, and the key stays C
A modulation to A minor, because G# appears and so the verse has left C major entirely

rubric: E7 is V7/vi: it leads to Am, and the tonal centre remains C because the rest of the section is diatonic.
Distractors over-read one accidental as a key change, misattribute the chord to C minor (which has Eb, not E), or deny chromatic chords that are common in diatonic songs.

items.prompt: A song is in C and its melody spans C4 to A4. The singer's comfortable range is A3 to F#4, and the guitarist wants an open-chord key (C, G, D, A or E). Which key best meets both criteria?
rubric: Down a minor third puts C4 on A3 and A4 on F#4, so the whole melody fits, and A is an open-chord key.
Bb leaves the top note too high, Ab and G drop the bottom note below A3, and Ab and Bb are awkward on guitar.

items.prompt: A student claims that parallel fifths are always an error. A guitarist's rock song moves its riff in parallel power chords (roots a fifth apart throughout). Which critique of the student's claim is most sound?

options.label: The rule protects independent voices in common-practice part writing, but parallel fifths are idiomatic in power-chord style
The rule is universal, so the guitarist should replace the power chords with parallel thirds to avoid error in any style
The rule applies only with four or more voices, so a two-note power chord can never break it in any style
The rule applies only to major keys, so a riff in a minor key is exempt from it and can move in fifths

rubric: The ban comes from the aim of keeping voices independent in common-practice writing; power chords deliberately fuse lines, so the criterion does not apply.
Distractors treat the rule as universal or invent mode- and voice-count exemptions that do not exist.

items.prompt: A band wants to modulate from C major to G major in the last chorus. Criteria: reach G smoothly through a chord common to both keys, then confirm the new leading tone F#. Which progression best meets them?
rubric: Am is vi in C and ii in G (the pivot), and D7 contains F#, confirming G major before arriving on G.
The other progressions stay in C or lack a pivot and the F# that signals the new key.

items.prompt: At bar 8 of a hymn-like tune in C major, the phrase must sound as if it is about to close but must not actually conclude. It must stay in key, and the bass must move by step. Which chord pair best meets the criteria?
rubric: G7 – Am is a deceptive cadence: the bass steps G to A and the expected tonic is withheld.
G7 – C and F – C close the phrase (and G7 – C has a bass leap), while C – G does not create the expectation of a close.

items.prompt: A soloist plays over G7 resolving to Cmaj7 and wants maximum tension on the G7. Criteria: the scale must contain the b9, #9, b5 and #5 of G7 and still pull toward C. Which scale best meets them?

options.label: G blues scale (G Bb C Db D F)

rubric: The altered scale contains Ab, Bb, Db and Eb (b9, #9, b5, #5) and resolves strongly to C.
Mixolydian has no altered tensions, Dorian has a minor third that clashes with the chord, and the blues scale lacks the b9 and #5.

items.prompt: In C major, an arranger wants to approach Dm with a chord that has dominant function and contains C#, the leading tone to D. Which chords meet both criteria? Select all that apply.
rubric: A7 (V7/ii) and C#dim7 (vii°7/ii) both contain C# and lead to D minor with dominant function.
Em7, Fmaj7 and G7 contain no C# and do not tonicise D.

items.prompt: A cover band plays a song in C major and wants a key change for the last chorus with no rehearsal time. The vocalist's top note is F5 and she cannot sing above G5. The change must be audible as a lift. Which option best meets the criteria?

options.label: Jump up a perfect fourth to F major, so the lift is large and her top note rises to Bb5
Jump up a whole step to D major, so the lift is audible and her top note rises only to G5
Move to the relative minor, A minor, so the key changes cleanly and her top note stays in reach
Jump up a minor third to Eb major, so the lift is strong and her top note rises to Ab5

rubric: Up a whole step raises F5 to G5, which is her maximum, and gives an audible lift.
A fourth or a minor third pushes the top note past G5, and the relative minor changes the mood but gives no real lift.

items.prompt: In C major, a progression runs Dm7 – Db7 – Cmaj7. Judged by how the chords actually behave, which analysis of Db7 (Db–F–Ab–Cb) is best?

options.label: A tritone substitute for G7, because both share the F–B tritone and the bass falls a semitone to C
A Neapolitan sixth chord, because its root is the lowered second degree and it leads into the tonic
A chromatic passing chord with no function, because Db is outside C major and cannot be analysed
A secondary dominant of Gb major, so the progression must pass through Gb before it can reach C

rubric: Db7 contains F and Cb (=B), the same tritone as G7, and its root moves down a semitone to C, so it is a tritone substitution.
The Neapolitan option confuses a major triad on b2 with a dominant seventh chord; the Gb option ignores that it resolves directly to C.

items.prompt: A keyboard maker needs one fixed tuning that lets players modulate freely to any key. Judged against that criterion, which justification for equal temperament is best?

options.label: It gives every key identical intervals, trading perfectly pure thirds for a small, uniform impurity that is tolerable everywhere
It tunes all twelve fifths pure, so the cycle of fifths closes exactly on the starting octave without any leftover
It keeps the best-sounding thirds in a few favoured keys, so remote keys are rarely needed in practice
It tunes every major third and fifth to pure whole-number ratios, so all keys are perfectly in tune at once

rubric: Equal temperament makes all keys equivalent by slightly detuning every interval except the octave, which is what free modulation needs.
The pure-interval and pure-fifths options ignore that pure tuning cannot close the circle (the comma); the favoured-keys option describes meantone.

items.prompt: A student labels the I6/4 chord before V at a cadence as 'a tonic chord in second inversion, so the phrase ends with a tonic prolongation'. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Sound: second inversion is more stable than root position, which reinforces its tonic function at the cadence
Flawed: it is really a predominant ii chord, because both of its upper notes resolve onward to the dominant
Sound: any triad on the tonic pitch has tonic function, and inversion never changes a chord's function
Flawed: its sixth and fourth above the bass behave as suspensions resolving to V's third and fifth, so it is dominant in function

rubric: The cadential 6/4 is a double suspension over the dominant bass: 6 falls to 5 and 4 falls to 3, so its function is dominant.
Treating it as tonic or as stable ignores that second inversion triads are unstable and need resolution.

items.prompt: In a score in A major, a melody rises chromatically from A to B in bar 1 and falls chromatically from B to A in bar 2. Judged by standard spelling conventions that keep the line readable, which spelling is best?

options.label: Rising A, Bb, B; falling B, A#, A
Rising A, A#, B; falling B, Bb, A
Rising A, A#, B; falling B, A#, A
Rising A, Bb, B; falling B, Bb, A

rubric: Convention spells ascending chromatic notes with sharps and descending ones with flats, so the accidental points the way the line moves.
The other options use the wrong direction or a single spelling for both directions, which obscures the line's direction.

items.prompt: A jazz player improvises over a G7 chord that resolves to Cmaj7. They want b9, #9, b5 and #5 available, while keeping the chord's third and seventh. Which scale best meets these criteria?
rubric: The altered scale (Ab melodic minor from G) contains b9, #9, b5, #5 plus the third and seventh.
Whole-tone lacks b9 and #9; half-whole diminished has a natural fifth and 13th instead of #5; Mixolydian has no altered tensions.

items.prompt: A student evaluates the Italian augmented sixth chord (F–A–D#) in A minor. Which claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.label: Its augmented sixth contracts inward to a fifth over the dominant bass
It substitutes for the tonic chord at a final cadence
F and D# resolve outward by step to an octave on E
It acts as a predominant chord that leads to V
It is enharmonically a dominant seventh chord, so it is a Italian-type variant of V7

rubric: The F–D# augmented sixth expands outward to the octave E–E, and the chord functions as a predominant resolving to V.
Enharmonic equivalence to a dominant seventh applies to the German type, not the Italian; the interval expands rather than contracts.

items.prompt: A band's song is in C major, and the arranger wants the last chorus in Eb major. The brief says the shift should sound smooth, use a pivot chord that is diatonic or familiar in both keys, and arrive with a clear dominant. Which plan best meets these criteria?

options.label: Pivot on F, then Bb7 into Eb, because F major is the subdominant in C and a normal chord in Eb
Pivot on Ab, then Bb7 into Eb, because Ab is a borrowed chord in C and diatonic as IV in Eb
Pivot on Am, then Bb7 into Eb, because Am is the relative minor and also a chord of Eb
Pivot on Dm, then Bb7 into Eb, because Dm lies a step above the tonic in both keys

rubric: Ab major is bVI borrowed from C minor and IV in Eb, so it works as a pivot before the Bb7 dominant.
Dm, F and Am are diatonic in C but not in Eb, since Eb contains Fm, Gm and Cm instead.

items.prompt: Brief: a five-chord progression in A minor that opens on the tonic, includes an augmented sixth chord as the predominant, and closes with a V7–i authentic cadence. Which progression meets every constraint?

options.label: Am – Dm – German sixth (F–A–C–D#) – E – Dm
Am – Dm/F – German sixth (F–A–C–D#) – E7 – Am

rubric: The German sixth on F (F–A–C–D#) is the predominant, resolves to E7, and the last chord is the tonic.
F7 with Eb is not an augmented sixth; the G7–C option has no augmented sixth; the last option ends away from the tonic.

items.prompt: An arranger needs a trumpet in Bb and an alto saxophone in Eb to both sound in concert Eb major. Which pair of written keys meets the brief?

options.label: Trumpet in D major, alto sax in C major
Trumpet in Eb major, alto sax in Eb major
Trumpet in F major, alto sax in C major
Trumpet in F major, alto sax in G major

rubric: Bb trumpet sounds a major second lower than written, so write F; Eb alto sounds a major sixth lower, so write C.
The other pairs transpose in the wrong direction or leave a part untransposed.

items.prompt: A student plans a harmonization in A minor using only natural-minor chords i, iv and v (Em), ending v–i. The brief demands an authentic cadence where a leading tone pulls to the tonic. What does the plan need?

options.label: Replace v with VII (G) so the bass descends by step into the tonic
Raise the seventh degree to G# so V is major and G# resolves up to A
Make the final chord A major so the ending feels resolved
Add Fmaj7 before the cadence so the lowered sixth moves to E

rubric: Raising the seventh (harmonic minor) makes V major and gives a leading tone G# that resolves to A.
VII–i is a subtonic cadence without a leading tone; a major final chord and Fmaj7 do not supply one.

items.prompt: Brief: write a four-bar melody for a round in which four voices enter one bar apart, so that all overlapping bars stay consonant. Which design meets this?

options.label: Make every bar outline the same tonic triad, with non-chord tones only as passing notes on weak beats
Use a different key signature for each bar so every entry starts from fresh material
Write a long tonic pedal in the first bar, then free chromatic lines in the remaining three bars
Change the implied chord every bar (I–IV–V–I) and use only chord tones of each bar's harmony

rubric: If every bar outlines the same harmony, any overlap of bars stacks the same triad, and weak-beat passing notes keep dissonance mild.
A changing progression produces clashes when bar 1 sounds against bar 3, and chromatic or key-shifting material breaks the overlap.

items.prompt: In 6/8 (eighth notes numbered 1–6, normally accented on 1 and 4), a composer wants one bar of hemiola that starts on the downbeat and feels like three groups of two. On which eighths should the accents fall?
rubric: Hemiola regroups six eighths as 2+2+2, accenting 1, 3 and 5 and starting on the downbeat.
1 and 4 is normal 6/8; 2, 4, 6 are offbeats and miss the downbeat requirement.

items.prompt: Brief: a two-chord vamp in D that must sound D Dorian rather than D natural minor, by sounding the characteristic raised sixth (B natural). Which vamps meet the brief? Select all that apply.
rubric: G major and Em7 both contain B natural, the Dorian sixth degree.
Bb and Gm7 contain Bb, the Aeolian sixth, and point to D natural minor.

items.prompt: Over a looping C – Am – F – G progression (one bar each), the singer sustains one long note per bar. An arranger must add a countermelody that moves while the melody holds, avoids parallel fifths and octaves with the bass, and stays tied to each chord. Which design best meets these constraints?

options.label: Hold a G pedal through all four bars so the line never clashes with the bass
Move mostly against the bass, landing on a chord third each downbeat (E, C, A, B) with stepwise passing notes between
Move in parallel fifths with the bass so the line has a strong harmonic anchor
Double the vocal an octave higher so the line reinforces every sustained note

rubric: Landing on chord thirds and moving in contrary motion ties the line to the harmony and avoids forbidden parallels.
Octave doubling adds no independent motion, a G pedal fights the F and Am chords, and parallel fifths violate the brief.
